name: Charles I of England
role: King of England, Scotland and Ireland (1625–1649)
summary: Charles I upheld a hereditary monarchy in which the king held the powers of war, appointment and assent within a mixed constitution of King, Lords and Commons, and rejected Parliament's claims to share in them. He backed an episcopal, uniform established church under Laud, ruled eleven years without calling an English Parliament, and denied that the people have a share in government. He refused to recognise the court that tried him in 1649.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Defended the House of Lords against restriction of the votes of peers 'whose blood give them' the right, and treated the powers of the Crown as hereditary.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Governed 1629-1640 without calling an English Parliament, raising revenue through ship money, monopolies, customs and fines instead.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Raised Laud to Canterbury in 1633 and, reportedly, made bishops the instruments of a uniform church across Britain, including the Scottish canons and prayer book.

consent-of-governed.rationale: On the scaffold he said the people's liberty lies in government under laws, not in a share in it, and that subject and sovereign are 'clean different things'.

democracy-best.rationale: The Answer lists the ills of democracy as tumults, violence and licentiousness and prefers a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy, so he did not hold democracy to be best.

direct-votes.rationale: On the scaffold he said it was 'nothing pertaining' to the people to have a share in government, and the Answer says the Commons was never intended for any share in government.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Told the court that he held a trust committed to him by God, by old and lawful descent.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Said that yielding the Houses' demands would depose both himself and his posterity and treated the Crown as a trust passed down by descent.

elective-rulers.rationale: Told the court he held his trust from God 'by old and lawful descent', and the Answer treats the Crown as an inheritance passing to his posterity.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Insisted that command of the militia and the commissions for raising men are the King's, and on the scaffold said the militia was his and the war began when Parliament took it.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Dissolved Parliament in 1629 when it passed the Three Resolutions and did not call another English Parliament until 1640.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The Answer praises England's constitution as a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy with the conveniences of all three and the inconveniences of none, and rejects any shift in the balance.

national-church-status.rationale: As king he made the Church of England the only legal church and pressed obedience to its prayer book as an essential pillar of royal government.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Answer warns that giving the Commons power over appointments would intoxicate persons who were not born to it, treating rule as a matter of birth.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Rejected the Houses' demands, holding the King has as much right to reject what Parliament proposes as it has to propose it, with legislation needing the King as one of three estates.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The record is split: he pursued revenue by reviving old laws and traditional ship money collected through local justices, yet extended it to the whole country, which many subjects thought illegitimate.

property-fundamental.rationale: Levied ship money, extended from ports to the whole country, plus monopolies and enforcement of old forest and enclosure rules to raise revenue without Parliament, which overrode owners' claims for the Crown's purposes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Denied that any court on earth could try a king, called his judges a usurped authority, and treated Parliament's resistance as rebellion rather than a right of the people.

second-chamber.rationale: Described the Lords as an essential part of the constitution, trusted with judicial power and acting as a screen and bank between prince and people.

separate-church-state.rationale: Under him and Laud the established church was made a pillar of royal government, with a single prayer book and uniformity of worship pressed on the Scottish church as well.

separated-powers.rationale: The Answer describes laws as made jointly by King, Lords and Commons, each with its own role, the Lords as a screen between prince and people, and each estate to run in its proper channel.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Split in his words: the Answer says the law ought to be the rule of King, Lords and Commons alike, but at his trial he held that a king cannot be tried by any superior jurisdiction on earth.

notes: Eikon Basilike was not used (attributed to Gauden). Laws he assented to under pressure (Petition of Right, Triennial Act, Strafford's attainder) are not counted as his positions. Themes searched: government, church, economy and taxation, world (the Answer's alliance clause, the Scottish wars), liberty and society; his surviving texts and the trial and scaffold speeches say little beyond constitution, church and militia, so most statements are null. Record answers rest on scholarly reports (Hyde, James), so are medium at most; sources that only cited Wikipedia in the first pass were dropped and the answers re-based on texts and scholarship.

booksNotUsed.reason: Eikon Basilike was published under his name but is attributed by modern scholarship to John Gauden, so it is not shown to be words he delivered as his own.
